Income Tax Act
$200,000 income. This is what is being done with our present tax structure. It would be wise to scrap the whole thing.
At the present time we require development in the Arctic. That development should take place where, when, and how it is needed. The government went a little way toward encouraging development. It set up Panarctic and the Canada Development Corporation. It has gone into development in a limited way, sometimes more, sometimes less. The government has not decided that the end product is jobs and that incentive must be provided to industries for that purpose. The government has attempted to provide jobs with a shotgun approach in order to make everyone a little bit happy, the result of which is that nothing has been done for most people.
I am reminded of what the former hon. member for Sudbury talked about in the House years ago. He was referring to insurance companies. He called them parasites, he called us parasites, and he went on to say that people who live off the workers are parasites.
Not long ago I listened to a speech by Mr. Doug Fisher, a former colleague. He pointed out that, according to Statistics Canada, there are 700,000 people in Canada working for a living, producing the wealth of this nation. These figures refer to miners, forest product workers, fishermen and farmers. He went on to point out that we have 2.5 million sales people in Canada. There are only 700,000 workers, but there are 2.5 million listed as sales persons, as well as over one million clerks. It makes one wonder, if we have that few people doing all the work and the rest of us living off them. Are teachers, politicians, salesmen, and advertisers living off the workers because they are not producing our nation's basic wealth? If we are to go ahead in this country, it must be in highly modernized and technical fields. At the present time one farmer can farm 1,000 acres, whereas before his father was hard pressed to farm more than 160 acres. We are highly mechanized and can outproduce other countries in most of our basic resources.
If we are to develop jobs for people, they should be in the manufacturing field. We must make a choice of a limited number of areas in which we should concentrate our research and development. The entire direction of the government should be toward that end. Perhaps the government will make a mistake in the choice of industries requiring research and development, but we will have to bear with it. It will be necessary to choose what industries should be developed, and hopefully some of the natural assets of this country will be used. The industries will have to be developed to a point where they can compete with anyone in the world who is involved in those fields. We need a government which is prepared to market our products, form trading blocs to negotiate with other countries, and use that system so that we have an opportunity to sell.
When I was in Cuba a year ago I was shocked by the number of small Ford Cortina automobiles on the streets. I asked why those automobiles bore a Spanish name. One official pointed out that Cuba had approximately 20,000 of those cars. They had attempted to order those cars in Canada,
(Mr. Peters.]
but Canadian Ford indicated that they could not be sold to Cuba because of a law in the United States. Thus, those 20,000 cars were purchased from Argentina instead. In any event Ford receives the money, but because of different arrangements in Argentina it was necessary for Cuba to purchase the 20,000 Ford Cortina automobiles there rather than in Canada. Perhaps it was not such a good deal, but if Argentina did not lose on it, why should Canada be prevented from becoming involved?
I am sure it was a shock for all hon. members, particularly cabinet ministers who realize that it is necessary for Canada to move goods, to learn that we had expertise in fields at one time which we no longer have. Canada is a very large country with the largest coastline in the world. We have to move goods. I remember that during the war we had one of the largest fleets in the world. We had developed a very large merchant navy. We put it together with haywire and tin cans, and all the rest of it. It may not have been so good, and the government was sure as hell interested in getting rid of it after the war. Do not forget that a lot of those ships, Fiberty ships in particular, went to Onassis. That is how Onassis built his fortune. That is how he got his multimillion dollar enterprise controlling a large part of the shipping world. He started it with our Fiberty ships which he bought for almost nothing because we wanted to get rid of them.
I was interested in attending at NATO. I am not really interested in NATO. They are carrying out a paper war. They move papers around like we do here, I suppose. They have tanks and all those other things. They were suggesting that if we had difficulty in Europe and the Russian overran us, we would be able to hold them off for two weeks and by then reinforcements would arrive. How will those reinforcements get there? Will they get there by aircraft? We do not have any transport planes that will carry a sizeable number of troops, and certainly will not carry equipment. We do not have any ships. At NATO they suggested we will use United States ships. Hell, the Americans will be there and will be using every bottom they can find, rent or borrow across the country to move the stuff they have to move. They will not be lending ships to Canada.
We were the experts at building ships. We had a reputation which had been built up over three or four hundred years of shipbuilding in this country, building everything from tea clipper ships to Fiberty ships. We were recognized and renowned as shipbuilders, the builders of fast, useful ships with good utility. We can build them, but the government got out of this enterprise because it decided we are not in that business. We were not interested in a merchant navy.
Norway did not say that. Norway did not have any ships. It decided it better get some because its people lived on the sea. Norway now has one of the largest merchant navies in the world. It seems to me if Canadians are going to move troops overseas, and everybody is talking about defence, then we better obtain some long range contracts with Norway in order
May 29, 1978

that we can rent some of their ships, because we do not have any. We could build ships that would sell in other countries.
Canada is a real big country. What are we doing playing around with airplanes? We have played around with the Twin Otter, The Beaver, and now the Dash-7, of which we have not sold any. Perhaps we have done better with the Lear jet. I presume that is the one that Canadair has, or a modification of that Lear jet. We may have done better with it because there is a market elsewhere.
We had probably the best team of aeronautical engineers in the world. We had a team in the aeronautical field that you would not believe could be built up by a country like Canada. We did not raise those people; we brought them in from elsewhere. Most Most of them came from Europe. They are not here now because they left and went to NASA. They really are the basis of the whole NASSAU operation. They were the areonautical brains of the world. We had more than our share. We did not steal many from Germany, but we sure got a lot from the British when they decided to go out of the airplane business. We lost all that, not because of anything those people did, but because of the fiasco of the government in relation to our air program.
We could have developed one of the best aircraft industries in the world. It is my honest opinion we could have built a transport plane that would have been useful to Canada in meeting Canadian needs. This likely would have had a spin-off in the military field. We did not move in that direction because we really did not make up our minds what field we wanted to move in. We really did not decide what industry we wanted to develop. We developed a branch plant economy related to the United States. In many ways this was not a bad economy as long as things were going up. When they started to go down, the parent companies weighed jobs against transportation costs and found it easier to ship things in than to develop them here and sell them. They pulled back on development in our country. This has happened in respect of many industries, particularly those which have an up and down attitude in relation to the economy.
We could go on with a discussion about what we are doing in respect of transportation. We could develop in a number of other fields in which we are obviously competent. We could develop a car in this country to meet the northern parts of a number of countries. Our needs are not unlike those of Sweden, Norway, Finland, the north part of England and parts of Japan. We could develop a car, just as other countries have done, if we concentrated on one or two cars and put an industry together, saying, to hell with the Americans, if they want to take their industries back to the United States we will build our own." I do not think we have much of a future in the automobile industry, because every time I listen to people talking about that industry I learn of another truck or automobile plant that is moving back to the United States. Perhaps we should not eliminate those branch plants, but we should start to develop a Canadian industry of our own. We have to be selective, and this must be a government supported effort with the co-operation of the provinces and the people.
Income Tax Act
We have to make war on unemployment in this country. There are many highly trained young workers in this country who have never worked. Often girls come to the office looking for jobs. They are just out of school, and hold degrees. We want people with typing skills and experience. We need people who have dealt with people on a one to one basis, and who know how people react, and how to talk to them. These people have had no experience. This is a very limited field, but this situation is true in many areas.
I heard farmers talking the other day about having young people come to work on the farm in the summer. After a while one farmer allowed a young lad to drive his tractor. He said he had two loads of hay on the wagon behind the tractor. He also had one of those little four wheel drive jimmies. He asked the 17 or 18 year old lad from town whether he could drive it. The lad said that he could, and the farmer told him to stay behind the tractor and wagon. He did stay behind for a short distance, but as soon as they reached a wider part of the road he drove by and down the road like crazy. He had obsolutely no sense when driving it, not understanding how it worked. He was lucky to arrive at his destination. The lad told his mother he would not mind working there for nothing because the farmer let him drive this vehicle.
It is not the boy's fault he has no experience. He is no dumber than anyone else, but he has had no opportunity to be around machinery or to operate it. He has no living experience. There are many young people today in this category.
If things get much tougher we will soon see gangs of these young people on the street, and they will eventually start the type of activity that is occurring in other countries of the world. We certainly do not need that sort of thing in Canada. This will not be entirely the fault of these young people, it will be the result of our own failures.
There is one other field where the government must implement a national strategy, and that is for industrial development. We have to get the people in the civil service working instead of pushing paper. I was speaking to a man on the plane this morning who described a situation to me. The government had established an extra district office and the people in the district office felt they were doing things about which they had no knowledge. He went on to outline a situation where he had bid on a tender for a garbage pail pad in this particular community. The pad was to be approximately eight feet long and four feet wide. His bid was $184. The government insisted that he get an architect and drawings. He told them to use their own people and build it themselves because he was not going to do that. The cost would have been around $2,000, where his bid had only been $184, to pour a couple of yards of concrete and to put a small amount of aggregate under it. This kind of situation illustrates what is occurring all over the country because all we are doing is moving paper.
I feel that where people are competent and well trained, we should be giving them an opportunity to develop an industrial strategy. We are better at these things than a lot of people

across the world. We are more competent, we have more initiative, and we certainly live in a colder climate where we have to do something at least to keep warm. We cannot just lie under the banana tree and get our food. We have shown our ability in the past, and we should give our young people an opportunity to participate in the future. This can only happen if the government puts forth an industrial strategy.
Recently I, along with other members, had discussions with the representative on tariffs who had returned from Geneva. Much of industry in Canada is involved with tariff protection, concessions, and subsidies. In listening to our representative, and I am sure the other members would come to the same conclusion, we are "babes in the woods". Mr. Speaker, it is becoming a pattern where my comments on matters of this sort are being interrupted by the bell to call it five o'clock or four o'clock. However, I must say that I sat back and wondered at the verbosity, articulateness, and inventiveness of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) in skirting around this bill. In fact I do not know if he is even aware of the number of the bill we are discussing because he dealt with such matters as national strategy for industrial development, a need to develop the aircraft industry more fully, and the merchant marine.
The merchant marine is an area in which the hon. member and I see eye to eye, and we deplore its loss. He went on in that particular stream very, very effectively. Then he jumped to productivity in the public service. Finally, before you called him to order, Mr. Speaker, because his time had run out, he was on GATT and the discussions in Geneva.
I would like to draw to the attention of the hon. member that the bill before us today, aside from being numbered C-56, is described as:
An act to amend the statute law relating to income tax-
It refers to income tax, Mr. Speaker, and he may have overlooked that because I do not think income tax was mentioned. It goes on:
-and to authorize payments related to provincial sales tax reductions-
We have to congratulate the hon. member on his enormous ingenuity in being able to talk as though it were either a debate on the Speech from the Throne or on the budget, and his ability to cover all those areas and to avoid the two principal matters before the House, namely, income tax and sales tax reductions.
I see the hour is approaching five o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to call it five o'clock so that I might begin my comments at eight o'clock.

It being five o'clock, the House will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely, notices of motions, public bills.

May 29, 1978

The House resumed from Monday, November 14, 1977, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre):
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to the advisability of amending the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to provide for the pensions payable under these two acts to be available at age 60 to all persons who meet the other requirements of the said acts and who are not in or are prepared to withdraw from the labour market, and also to provide for the basic amount of the pension payable under the Old Age Security Act, at age 60 for those not in the labour market and to everyone at age 65, to be increased to $300 per month, for this basic amount to be escalated each year by an amount that will enable pensioners not only to keep up with rising living costs but to share in rising living standards, and also to provide for the elimination of any means or income test from the Old Age Security Act, so that the full pension thereunder will be recognized as the established right of all our people.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION PENSION BE PAID TO PERSONS AT AGE 60 UNDER CERTAIN CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to participate in this debate on the motion by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has demonstrated his keen understanding and sensitivity on the issue of pensions. His concern is shared on this side of the House by Liberal members who have expressed their support for this particular issue, in caucus and in their own ridings. It was the thinking of this government back in the sixties, which has allowed Canada to have perhaps one of the finest social security systems that exist in the world today.
One goes back to the Pearson years when this was possible. It was a Liberal administration that introduced the Canada Pension Plan as we know it, as well as the Medicare system. These were two very important steps taken on a long road of Liberal measures which included the Old Age Security Pension, the Guaranteed Income Supplement, and Hospital Insurance back in the 1950s. It would be quite correct to say that Canadians today look to parliament for social security protection as a continuation of these fine traditions established by Liberal governments.
Old Age Security
The motion recommends that the old age pension be increased to $300 per month. There are arguments that could be made about the effect of such an increase on retirement savings. I am sure every member of the House would be in favour of it, particularly if it did not cost the taxpayer anything. At this point the debate becomes somewhat controversial because we all have different notions about whether the taxpayer can stand an additional load. We hear the Conservative party say that government spending should be reduced, and that taxes should be reduced. It would therefore be consistent that anything pertaining to an increase in benefit payments would require a substantial change in the policies of the official opposition. On this side of the House we like to think that as wealth is created and generated in the country it will be distributed properly and find its way to those members of society who need basic protection, either because of age or disability.
While I support the basic thrust of the hon. member's motion which is to make the pension available at a lower age, I would prefer that rather than fixing an age-the hon. member recommends 60-the qualifying age for old age security be made flexible. I think of people working in industries that are physically demanding and which wear out the worker sooner than other industries. People working in mines or construction, for instance, often have to do heavy lifting. The jobs are demanding from a physical point of view, and there is often a desire to retire sooner than people engaged in activities not so physically demanding. Perhaps it should be left to the individual to decide on his retirement age. If someone wished to retire sooner, conceivably he could draw a smaller pension than the person who wished to retire later.
In a democracy, we could surely develop a system that would leave options open to the individual. A pension system seems to be a logical place to provide for this flexibility and these options. There may be those who would wish or would need to retire at age 49, 11 years earlier than the age of 60 provided in the motion. And, of course, there may be people who would wish to retire later than 60. There is a trend in certain occupations and professions these days for later retirement. I would link this trend to the kind of work an individual performs.
As we move into the eighties-and perhaps even sooner-we should conceive a system to allow the individual to make a decision on his own, depending on his personal circumstances and the conditions that prevail in his profession or occupation. A system of nailing future legislation to a fixed age level is not as desirable as a system that would allow individuals to retire sooner if they wished but, of course, at a lower level of pension.
I should like to deal also with one aspect of the Canada Pension Plan which deserves to be given consideration in this debate and I commend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for having put forward this comprehensive motion that permits us to debate this matter in its entirety.
In the past, some people have not qualified for a disability pension under the Canada Pension Plan because they had not

May 29, 1978
Old Age Security
made the necessary five years of contributions. A situation could conceivably arise where someone contributed for four years and nine months but was denied a disability pension because the magic figure of five years had not been reached. I can understand the need for certain minimum contributions, but I suggest a change should be made. At times we may come across a situation that is very serious where, as a result of a highway or other accident that is not compensated by provincial legislation such as workmen's compensation, a person does not qualify for disability pension. We should make a change so that such person would receive a disability pension in proportion to the number of years he contributed to the scheme. For instance, if he had contributed for three years instead of the prescribed five, he ought to be allowed to draw a partial or reduced pension. The same would apply to a contribution that would reflect a shorter period of time.
Even if this were very modest in substance, it would still be better than the complete denial that a contributor has to accept under the present legislation when the contribution falls short, even by one day, of the prescribed five years.
The Canada Pension Plan could also be a vehicle for new approaches to the whole idea of a basic social security system. It seems to me there are a number of occupations which are not covered right now but deserve at least the benefit of a study to determine how they could be covered. For instance, there are a number of individuals in this country who would be glad to contribute the employee's contribution plus the employer's contribution to the Canada Pension Plan. I suspect they would be willing to make the total contribution, namely, the employer-employee portions, even a larger monthly contribution than the present one if they were allowed to do so if eventually this would lead to qualifying under the Canada Pension Plan for retirement and other coverages that are envisaged under this plan.
At the present time women raising their children are not allowed to contribute to the Canada Pension Plan. In other words, if a spouse is raising children and is not in the labour force, this leads to an exclusion which one can perhaps understand within the narrow confines of the law. But in broader social terms I cannot understand why a citizen who is willing to make a full contribution, namely, that of an employee plus that of the employer, at his or her own expense, ought not to be allowed to do so and then be allowed eventually to draw some benefits.
Although I cannot prove it because I have not had an opportunity to do the necessary research, I suspect that the number of people wishing to enter the labour force would be lower, namely, the so-called participation rate. People entering the labour force would not be doing so quite so dramatically as they have done these past few years if they were allowed to contribute as do those presently in the labour force. It stands to reason that if a person is at home and wondering about his future and his retirement income and not in the labour force, that person would not be contributing to the Canada Pension
[Mr. Caccia.l
Plan as it stands now. Then that person would begin to wonder if he or she should not enter the labour force-to contribute to the family income in the first place-but at the same time as a thought and as a possibility one must anticipate the time of retirement, and that thought goes together with the thought of being in the system and of being allowed to contribute among other things to the Canada Pension Plan. Otherwise this cannot be done and that person cannot qualify, let's say in this case, for the provision of the old age pension that comes from this particular plan which, added to the old age security pension, gives a greater degree of assurance about the time when one retires and has to depend on a fixed income for retirement years.
It seems to me that in a society as we know it in Canada there ought to be, in the total scheme of things having to do with pensions and social security, a greater degree of flexibility. This flexibility ought to be coupled with a greater number of options which can be given to the individual. Perhaps I will sum it up in this form.
If one wants to receive a pension earlier in life, one could choose that route, excepting of course that one would receive a smaller pension by drawing it sooner. Secondly, as to the possibility of being a contributor to an important scheme, such as Canada Pension Plan, one should be allowed to contribute and be part of the system even when one is not an employee and therefore not in the labour force. This could be done by creating a special category, or a category that simply permits one to make a full contribution, namely, the employer's plus that of the employee. This would allow a person to continue whatever important role that person performs in the home, which we all recognize.
Others are perhaps more qualified to make a better speech on this subject. People not in the labour force would get this sense of security when permitted to be part of the system, and allowed to contribute to it, enabling them to make plans for the future and for that day which will inevitably come of having to live on a fixed income.

At the outset I would like to state that from this side of the House we find much that is commendable in the motion put forward. Like the hon. member who has just spoken, and the hon. member who has proposed this motion, I am sure that every member in this House has had representations, generally and particularly from time to time, especially during the last two or three years of difficult economic conditions involving the younger segment of the population. Like hon. members on both sides of the House on many occasions I have received representations that it is too bad that so many older people are working when they really do not have to, and when there is such a high unemployment rate among young people. I agree with the proposition that there is an incredibly high unemployment rate among younger people, but I am not sure that this is a good argument in itself per se for reducing the pensionable age to, let us say, 60 years of age.
Let me repeat what I said. Based on the argument that it is the younger breadwinner who should be given precedence in terms of employment as against the older worker, I wish to put forward my opinion that this, per se, is not an entirely valid argument.
I agree with the hon. member who put forward this proposition vis-a-vis the means test. I had hoped and thought many years ago that in relation to most social policy, especially in the area of pensions, we had gotten away from most if not every consideration relating to the means test.
I listened with great interest to the hon. member who put forward his ideas in a very constructive way. He asked for flexibility as we approach this subject, especially in relation to the age of 60. I think we are going to need that kind of flexibility.
I am not sure that I have the answer. I certainly do not want to go back to the means test, and I am not sure the computer has the answer in terms of finding us some middle ground between universality and the means test in terms of selecting those who, at the age of 60, by need and by desire, as the hon. member who just spoke said, should be drawing a pension at that age. While I want to get away entirely from any consideration of a means test, especially in the area of pensions, I think we have to look at this age of 60 on another basis than universality.
I approach this whole debate with one thing in mind especially. At the turn of the century we had not developed a sophisticated pattern of humane and decent delivery of medical and health care services. In this part of the western world, largely because of infant mortality, and the international definition of infant mortality being the death of a child between birth and one year, the average life expectancy of both males and females in North America was somewhere around 43 years of age. Today, largely because of the advances in humane, decent, and civilized medical and health care services, we now have a life expectancy of somewhere around

70 for males and 76 for females. I could be wrong in terms of exact years, but I believe it is generally around 70 for males and 76 for females.
The life expectancy was somewhat higher during the sixties and possibly the early seventies. However, because we have not come to grips in terms of cleaning up our environment-soil, water and air-in the last 12 years life expectancy for both males an females has gone down somewhere in the neighbourhood of one year.
In approaching this general subject, all members on both sides of the House should stop, look, and listen. It is my firm conviction that between now and the twenty-first century, based on my optimistic presumption, we will continue to make large advances in the delivery of decent and humane medical and health care services.
I join with the hon. member who made this proposition. There are members of that party who are largely responsible for many of our advances to date. I obviously think of the ex-leader of that party who had a lot to do with medicare in Saskatchewan. There is no excuse why we in Canada should not be able to say why we are not delivering the most decent, civilized, and humane social welfare and medical and health care services. However, in this case we must stop, look, and listen.
This is the most important point I can put forward in debate today. I realize there has been a lag in the last two years, but if we continue to finance medical health care and research properly, not only in terms of pure research but in terms of delivering medical and health care services at the community level, we will continue to make large advances. Between now and the turn of the century, there will be great advances in the area of cardiovascular disease treatment. I do not say that between now and nine o'clock tomorrow morning we will come up with an over-all cure for cancer. However, in terms of treatment and cures for certain aspects of cancer, notably breast cancer, great advances will be made.
We must come to terms with the greatest killer of our youth under the age of 35. I refer to highway and automobile deaths and injuries. While cancer may be the biggest killer, and cardiovascular disease second, or it could be the other way around, the biggest killer of our youth under the age of 35 is in or by automobiles. It is our third biggest killer in our country. Dr. Wilder Penfield and many other neurosurgeons in the western world call this an uncontrolled epidemic which is compounding itself by 8 per cent every year.
It is my belief that between now and the beginning of the twenty-first century we are going to come to terms with cardiovascular disease, many aspects of cancer, and we are going to get a handle on highway and automobile deaths and injuries.
Without getting into the crystal ball and tossing irresponsible figures into the air, I believe that while life expectancy has gone from 43 to over 70 up until now, by the turn of the century it will be somewhere around 86 years of age. I know a

lot of people joke and say they do not want to live that long, but the facts are that.
A bill like this should be analysed in terms of broad, social policy, realizing the advances that will be made in environmental medicine and preventive medicine, with a dramatic increase in life expectancy between now and the turn of the century.
I know the hon. member who put forward this bill is deeply sincere about it. He is very concerned about social and medical and health care policy. However, the bill should not only be analysed in terms of the fact that this government has messed up the economy of the country, that we have terrible youth unemployment and therefore terrible pressure is put on older Canadians to get out of the labour market. I sympathize with the decent spirit of the hon. member when he put forward this proposition, but it would be irresponsible for us to block ourselves rigidly into such a policy at this time without considering the long terms prospects of our aging population.
There are many charges on the treasury-federal, provincial and municipal-in terms of education costs. We are now educating a lot of our population past the age of 30. We are going to pension these same people off at age 60. In all fairness, without being ultra-conservative about it, I would ask the hon. member whether he has costed putting the retirement age of 60 under a universal program, because in terms of other priorities in the social and health field, one wonders where this priority would fit.
Because of the economic mess we are in at the present time, is there any money in the treasury for this kind of social thrust? I am not going to say that because this government has messed up the economy we should not take positive, creative and constructive steps in the social welfare and medical health care fields, but in terms of other priorities-preventive medicine, community medicine and all those things we should be doing in the social services bill which is soon to be brought before parliament in terms of day care centres, crisis intervention and that kind of thing-I wonder if the hon. member who proposed this measure has really thought about where this very costly measure should fit in the scheme of priorities. I wonder if he has thought about my deep conviction that, by the turn of the century, as I have said, the average Canadian and the average individual in the western world will be living to his or her mid-eighties. I reiterate that I quite agree with the hon. member that in many cases people could and should for many reasons retire at 60, but should this be a rigid, universal program? It is very clear that every member who has addressed the House recently on the subject of retirement has expressed different opinions. What is becoming increasingly important is that, while we are all striving to reach a common goal, namely, the well-being of Canadians, the objective is being approached by a great variety of seemingly contradictory routes.
It was recently that the House was debating the motion to consider the advisability of enacting legislation to raise the compulsory retirement age from 65 to 70 for any person aged 65 or more who does not wish to retire and is prepared to give up his or her entitlement to any private pension plan or annuity. Today we are asked in part to give consideration to the advisability of amending the Old Age Security Act and the Canada Pension Plan to provide for pensions payable under these two acts to be available at age 60 to all persons who meet the requirements of the said acts and who are not in, or are prepared to withdraw from the labour market.

The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) asked a pertinent question about the cost of the program envisaged by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). In the time remaining in the hour allotted for private members' business, I think that is a good point for discussion.
Let us look at the proposed increase in old age security benefits. The old age security program expended close to $4.5 billion in the 1976-77 fiscal year, roughly $3.3 billion of which was spent on the basis OAS benefit program, $1 billion on the guaranteed income supplement and $0.1 billion on the spouse's allowance.
Since there are at present just over two million old age security recipients in Canada, a $1 increase in the OAS pension implies a cost increase of more than $24 million annually. The member's motion proposes that the Old Age Security basic benefit be raised to $300 per month from its present amount of $156.66, almost doubling the current rate. It was easy to calculate that two million pensioners each receiving $300 per month or $3,600 per year would be paid $7.2 billion per year altogether. It was noted that this would represent a rise in total program expenditures of roughly $3.8 billion, or 84 per cent greater than the present cost.
As well, the member proposes that the income test currently applied to the guaranteed income supplement be removed. It is not entirely clear from the motion whether the benefit would be incorporated in the $300 he proposes, or tacked on to this

amount. If we make the latter assumption, all OAS pensioners over 65 would be entitled to the full GIS benefit in addition to the $300 per month basic pension. This was worked out to a total expenditure of roughly $2.4 billion at present rates, or $1.4 billion more than current GIS expenditures. The total OAS program expenditures would therefore rise by about $5.2 billion per year at current rates, if the benefit increases suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre are applied to the over 65 population, bringing the total program cost to $9.7 billion.
The hon. member suggests also that benefits under both the old age security program and the Canada Pension Plan should be made available at age 60 to those not in the labour market. This is, in effect, the reinstatement of the retirement test which the Canada Pension Plan formerly applied at age 65. However, it would apply at age 60. It is estimated that this measure alone would increase old age security costs by another $4 billion annually, making the total cost for this program $13.7 billion per year, or nearly treble the present total annual cost of the OAS program.
If legislation were introduced to allow CPP retirement pensions to be payable at age 60 in 1979, and if we assume that only half the eligible population takes advantage of early CPP retirement, we find that benefit payments would rise by $40 million in 1979 and would cost the Canada Pension Plan fund an extra $640 million by 1985.
If cost calculations are to reflect with any degree of accuracy the potential effect of these measures on the Canadian economy, they must go beyond a simple counting of increases in numbers of pensions and the dollar amount of benefits paid. We must bear in mind the rather obvious fact that an increase in the number of pensions means a corresponding decrease in the number of people in the labour force who must pay the taxes and contribute to support the larger population of pensioners. That is to say, we are not simply increasing by five the number of years for which the eventual pension must be paid; also we are lowering by five the number of years in which the individual contributes toward the benefits of others.
Then there are other hidden costs associated with lowering retirement ages and increasing benefits on which we can only speculate at this time. If income security benefits such as old age security are drastically increased, will this encourage people to be more dependent on public pensions and to decrease their personal retirement savings? I have been waiting for some time now to comment on the constitutional morass into which the government has stumbled, if, indeed, it has stumbled and not gone there of its own free will by design and where, as a matter of fact, it seems likely to sink or at least get itself frightfully mired down as a result of cooking up the $85 Quebec taxpayers deal that has so enraged not only Quebec but all the provinces of Canada. I will deal at length with this further blunder, the consequences of which can only be to drive a wedge more deeply between the federal government and the provinces.
It is tempting, Mr. Speaker, to ridicule the government for its apparent insensitivity in this area, a government made up of a party which has claimed for ten years now to be the only party capable of dealing with Quebec. Canada as a whole, however, is the principal casualty. Therefore, ridicule is just not the response that is called for by this particular issue.
Indeed, my approach is one of sorrow for Canada because of what this government is doing and seems bent on doing. The truth of the matter, of course, is that the vast majority of those making up this government are too close to Quebec to be in a position to take an unimpassioned approach to the problems contemporary Quebec has raised in Canada as a whole. This is not only in general constitutional terms but even in terms of this tax deal, which has become such an issue. They have convinced themselves that the proposal they have advanced in this legislation is compensatory in the sense that if, in a somewhat different way, it is doing in Quebec and for Quebeckers what it has already done for the other provinces and the inhabitants of those provinces, then it is right. There is no comparison. It is a completely new approach to the problem. It has to be, otherwise this legislation would not contain clause 59, which is the first subject of my comments.
This is a money raising bill with a clause providing for the outlay of funds. This matter has already been raised in the House, but it is a strange procedure that in a bill, primarily concerned with raising money, there is a provision, the last one, dealing with the spending of money. For all other provinces it was a matter of vacating part of the income tax field for each taxpayer, $100 worth to be exact, so that the province could occupy it. The taxpayer, of course, gains nothing out of that particular shift from one payee to another. This book transfer has been done in most of the provinces.
However, we must recall that the federal tax collecting agency, Revenue Canada, which at the moment is not represented in the House by a minister, does not collect income tax for the province of Quebec. Quebec assesses and collects its own income tax, and that is a distinguishing feature which we have to bear in mind. The federal government, however, was not going to allow the provinces to replenish their treasuries, generally speaking, leaving Quebec aside for the moment, without some quid pro quo on the part of the provinces that benefited thereby. The provinces were expected in return for that extra revenue which they were going to get to cut provincial sales tax levies by 3 per cent for six months. My

own province of British Columbia opted to cut the levy by 2 per cent for nine months.
The provinces gain revenue, on the one hand, by getting into the income tax room vacated by the federal government, but they lose revenue on the other by collecting less in the way of sales tax. It looks pretty fair and sounds like a good deal, and it probably was until the "feds" started fiddling around with the Quebec situation because Quebec had said, "Not on your life" to the proposition put forward by the federal government. They did so on the ground that the sales tax was provincial jurisdiction and the "feds" had no right whatever to suggest how the province can impose or collect its sales tax, a simple constitutional reply. I would say it is fair constitutional ball. I remind the House that the federal income tax collecting agency, Revenue Canada, does not collect the provincial income tax assessed in Quebec.
Thus, we had on the one hand several provinces agreeing to lower their sale tax and, on the other hand, Quebec refusing to do so in the across the board manner as proposed by the federal government. Instead, Quebec eventually decided in its own budget and within its own jurisdiction to drop the sales tax entirely but only on certain classes of goods that are manufactured in Quebec so as to benefit the manufacturers in that province-shoes, clothing, textiles and furniture. Their object was to preserve employment in those industries. Having done this, the Quebec tax authority asked for its prorated portion of the income tax deduction from which the other provinces had benefited, a sum amounting to approximately $186 million.
By this time the situation had become really complicated. The federal government refused the Quebec counter-proposition and claimed that the province had failed to co-operate. Things went ding-dong from it, and then the federal government hit on the novel idea that is set forth in this bill-to return as direct payments to Quebec taxpayers the amount they might have otherwise had returned to them had the provincial government played ball like the other provinces.
To get the picture properly into perspective, Mr. Speaker, I would like to read into the record an excerpt from a letter which was sent by the federal Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to the provincial minister of finance in Quebec. The Minister of Finance in his paragraph three starts out:
In your letter of April 27, you indicated that you did not accept the federal counter-proposal . .. The federal government has therefore decided to pay the Government of Quebec, as it undertook to do on April 21, an amount equivalent to two percentage points of the selective eliminations of the sales tax that you announced, that is, about $40 million. In order to rebate the remaining $186 million, the federal government will temporarily withdraw from the personal income tax field by reducing the tax paid by Quebec taxpayers by a corresponding amount.
For the Quebec taxpayer, this reduction will be equal to the lesser of $85 or the tax otherwise payable. The purpose of the rebate is to compensate Quebec taxpayers for the provincial sales tax which they will have to pay on all items not subject to a reduction from 8 to 6 per cent for six months.
This was the proposal made to the other provinces. Going to the next paragraph:
The sum of the $40 million to be paid to the Quebec Treasury for the selective eliminations of the sales tax and the $186 million to be rebated to Quebec

taxpayers corresponds to the $226 million allocated to Quebec in the Budget speech.
There we see the arrangements that were proposed, counter-proposed and finally laid down by the federal Minister of Finance.
There are several interesting features arising from this unusual proposal and they deserve mention. First of all, it provides a tax rebate to Quebeckers that was not provided to the citizens of the other provinces, $186 million worth if I read this correspondence correctly. In the case of the other provinces, hon. members will remember that the federal government vacated an area of income tax that was immediately reoccupied by the provinces. No citizens from the other provinces gained by this process; they were merely being taxed by a different authority at a different rate, sometimes higher, sometimes lower.
Second, the 3 per cent reduction of sales tax on purchases within a province benefits all citizens buying items subject to sales tax, from cars to stereos to building supplies to drug items. The elimination of the sales tax in Quebec benefits only those who buy shoes, clothing, furniture and textiles. But that is Quebec's decision and if Quebeckers do not like it as a long term thing they know what they can do-they can vote on it at the next general election in Quebec.
Third, the federal proposal will extend up to an $85 rebate to income tax payers only in Quebec. The Quebecker who pays no income tax will not benefit. That is an important point. It is favouritism of the worst sort. The revenue collected in other provinces as a result of the federal government vacating part of the income tax field will become part of the province's general revenue and as such will go to pay citizens in those provinces. No amount of casuistry can produce arguments to convince me that what is being done for Quebeckers is the same as was done under the tax vacating process for other provinces.
There are two jokers in this pack, Mr. Speaker. There are a lot more jokers than that with all the government members who are not over there! The first one is that on October 15, when the tax vacating deal plus the sales tax reduction notion comes to an end, the provinces will have to decide whether to continue with the sales tax reduction or suffer the political consequences of reimposing it. That is a nice way to deal with the provinces; it is a neat political trick to go through the motions of producing what looks like a favourable deal for the provinces with the full knowledge that the unfavourable consequences when the concession comes to an end will be borne by the provinces.
Is this the way to run a federation? Is this the way to treat federal-provincial relations-through Machiavellian trickery? Does the six-month deal and the October termination deal have anything to do with a general election? I think it is enough to make one wonder. One has every reason to ask why, if this government really wanted to do something positive to stimulate consumer buying, which presumably was at the bottom of this whole operation-the assumed reason for luring

the provinces into dropping their sales tax-it did not reduce the federal sales tax. They are losing $100 per taxpayer to the provinces as a general thing, at no gain to the taxpayer. Federal revenue, therefore, has dropped. Could it not have dropped by the same amount by reducing the federal sales tax? What mischief is this government about, what tortuous reasoning takes place within its councils, are questions the Canadian people have to ask.
I said there were two jokers in the pack. The second one may take a few words of explanation but it produces a surprising result. Quebeckers are to receive an income tax rebate of up to $85 because it proved impossible for the federal government to work out an income tax and sales tax deal with Quebec similar to the one worked out with the other provinces. That is, $85 on a six month deal that in most provinces produced a reduction of 3 per cent in sales tax across the board. It means, for those who get the $85, that they would have to purchase $2,833 worth of taxable goods in six months,
3 per cent of $2,833 being $85. Are income tax paying Quebeckers likely to buy that amount of taxable goods in six months aside from clothes, textiles, shoes and furniture? Is anyone? On top of that, Quebeckers get the benefit of total sales tax exemption when buying those items on which the Quebec government decided to eliminate the sales tax. It is a great deal-a great way to promote harmony in a federation!
The distressing conclusion to be drawn from this sorry mess in which we find ourselves is that this government seems determined to look always for political profit in its dealings with Quebec, and this time has failed utterly. The approach of the provincial legislature, voting unanimously to reject the proposal, is evidence of that.
We are bound to ask ourselves, as we have asked often and will ask as long as this government is in power, is this any way to hold a federation together-by exploiting a national crisis for political advantage? The answer obviously is no, it is not. Error heaped on error heaped on error: that is the record of this government. Once again I ask, how long are we to endure this "reign of error"?
Enough, however, of criticism. Surely there is something commendable in the bill before us. There is, even if it is not wholly commendable. I want to turn to clause 34 of the bill which has 19 long and tortuous subsections, all dealing with RRSPs and all arising out of paragraph 16 of the ways and means motion tabled by the Minister of Finance on April 10, 1978.
The first thing I want to say about this is that the motion broadens considerably the options open to those who have decided to make provisions for their retirement years by investing in RRSPs. I think this is a good thing. Prior to the tabling of the motion those who followed this route had only one option open to them aside from cashing in the savings in one fell swoop and facing the income tax consequences of doing so. Those consequences could be fairly heavy. That option was to convert those savings at any time between ages 60 and 71 into an annuity on which, of course, the annual levy of income tax would be paid.

It is worth recalling for a moment or two what the RRSP is all about. When originally conceived about 20 years ago the plan was designed to provide the self-employed person-the small business operator, the doctor, the garage owner, the lawyer-with an advantage already within reach of the salaried worker and the daily wage earner, namely, a tax exempt reduction in take home pay in order to build up a pension fund that could be drawn on upon retirement. Self-employed entrepreneurs were unable at that time to make provision for their retiring years and get a tax benefit as well. The RRSP provided that facility.
Over the years the emphasis on RRSPs seems to have shifted somewhat, just as the principle underlying the unemployment insurance scheme has shifted under this government. Whereas unemployment insurance was originally devised as an insurance to provide against the day when a salaried worker or daily wage earner found he was temporarily out of work, it has since become a means of collecting welfare entitlements that contributors are more and more coming to feel are their due. Having paid, they have to collect, just as the man who has paid fire insurance on his house for, say, 20 years decides in the 21st year that he is going to get his money back and sets fire to his house.
Something of the same sort has happened to the RRSP facility. Whereas it was originally designed as a pension planning scheme-a temporary relief from income tax on the funds being put aside-it is now tending to become a tax shelter with an incidental pension benefit. Everybody is getting into the act because the tax shelter benefit is there, even those who already have pension plans prepared for them by their employers under salary or wage deduction schemes.
The reasons for this shift from the pension scheme idea to the tax shelter notion are easy enough to understand. First of all, inflation has gripped most of us with its long entwining finger and threatens to throttle us, meaning fear for economic security in the years ahead which in turn dictates additional pension revenue than that provided by employers. Furthermore, the income tax cut by the government has been biting deeper and deeper into current income. So why not run for the nearest tax shelter, that of the RRSP?
RRSPs have become a way of saving for the future as well as saving oneself from the full burden of current taxes, with special emphasis on the latter advantage.
In his budget provisions in April the Minister of Finance responded in a sort of way to many of the representations that had been made to him to broaden the options open to the owner of an RRSP. These representations, so far as I can make out, were made by individuals but also by trust companies who, until that time, were unable to retain the use of the RRSP funds that may have drifted their way during the savings period of a working man's life. All annuities up until now had to be provided by the insurance companies. Individuals could save in a trust company but when it came time to roll that money over into an annuity, it had to go into an insurance

company. The April budget now opens the door for a type of annuity payment that can be handled by trust companies who will in future be offering competition to the insurance companies. I am assured by those to whom I have spoken that the insurance companies welcome this particular competition.
This broadening of the investment horizons comes about largely because of a new vehicle proposed in the budget that may be used by the retiree any time between age 60 and 71. This is the RRIF, the registered retirement income fund, into which the RRSP owner may roll his savings.
The options now open to the RRSP owner are as follows: Firstly, he may cash in his RRSP and meet his income tax obligations at one fell swoop if he wants to. That is option number one and it is not new.
Secondly, he may buy an annuity for life, a straight life annuity, or a term certain, say a 15-year or 20-year annuity. These he must still buy through an insurance company. That is option number two and it is not new.
Thirdly, he may buy an annuity equal to the number of years remaining between the age when he buys it and age 90. For example, if he buys it at age 60 he buys a 30-year fixed term annuity and it will be paid for as long as the annuitant lives. It will be paid certainly for 30 years, and if he should die, then it expires. That is option number three which extends the fixed term feature of annuities and it is new.
Fourthly, he may roll over his RRSP into a registered retirement investment fund which he himself can manage, if he so desires, or which he can have managed for him by any trust company, even the one in which he had invested the RRSP. The payments from that fund may be drawn down annually until age 90 in quantities determined in the law. It is an ingenious scheme that gradually works up in such a way to a good deal more at the end than at the beginning and finally sees the total extinction of the fund in the pensioner's 90th year. That is option number four and it is totally new.
One thing worth nothing about these options is that whichever option is selected it cannot be acted upon before the age of 60 and must be acted on by age 71. Comments on these limitations would appear to be in order. There is a third age at issue here and that is the age of 90 which deserves some comment.
In connection with age 60 the following remarks are warranted. Why is it not possible to get the RRSP, without loss, before 60 with the same options? Suppose a self-employed entrepreneur, the owner of a plumbing fitments business or of a garage, or a doctor or a lawyer, wants to retire at 55, or even 50 if he has made a good thing of it. Perhaps an individual has had an illness and had to retire earlier than age 60. If he has been laying RRSPs aside regularly during his working life, why should he be denied access to them except under penalty-that is, with some considerable loss? Is it because public servants who have devised these schemes are unwilling to see anyone retire before they do and set age 60 down as the earliest age at which contributors may gain access to their funds?

I think the arbitrary age of 60 is nonsense and that that limit might well be removed. The size of the fund will obviously be less because it will not have been invested as long. I can see no reason whatever why, with notice, the funds should not be available with the same or even more options whenever the investor wants it, whether it is before 60 or after.
At the other end of that 60 to 71 time limit why should anyone have to roll over his savings at age 71? 1 see no reason at all. Maybe an investor finds himself comfortable financially at age 71 and is prepared to let his money go on growing. Why should he not be able to do so? Why should he be obliged to roll over his RRSP into an annuity? At 75 he may feel like a world cruise or decide to cash in his RRSP. Why shouldn't he? Perhaps some of his other investments have not panned out as expected and at 75 or 78 he needs extra support. Maybe inflation has caught up with him. It could happen. In other words, why should he not be able to defer the roll over of his RRSP until he wishes? Or, as in the case of the lower end of that age bracket, why should he not get those funds without penalty when he wants them at age 55, 58 or even 50?
My other comment concerns age 71 and the fourth option, which is a self-managed fund. It is a pretty ridiculous proposal when you look at it. In 99 cases out of 100, who at 71 and over that age until reaching the age of 90 will be able to manage his own investment fund? It takes a very long life of studying the markets in order to be able to make a fund grow. If he does, can his trust company know with any certainty what the annual pay-outs will be? As one commentator in the Financial Post said on April 15:
This is going to turn the industry on its ear. Can you imagine the absolute chaos caused by an RRIF owner being able to run his own account but the trustee (i.e. the Trust Company) having at the same time to liquidate the fund according to a strict formula year by year?
Self-administered RRIFs at any age sound to me to be self-defeating. At age 71 they would probably be self-liquidating in the majority of cases.
Now, this age 90 limit brings me to my final comment. Many people live beyond 90. Life expectancy at 71 is nearer 85, true. But some die before 85, and some obviously live to 90 and beyond. Figures available to me indicate that in 1976, for example, there were 52,160 Canadians living over the age of 90.
These options nearly all close at age 90. The only one that does not, of course, is the life annuity option. This is the first one, the payment of an annuity for the life of the annuitant, be that for one or for 40 years. But even under this option presumably-at least this is the way I read the bill-an individual can contract with an insurance company for a period certain plus a life annuity which could carry the annuitant beyond age 90 should he live beyond that age.
Options three and four, however, foreclose at age 90. Why? Not only why, but what happens after age 90, for those who live that long? Who chose the mystic 90 figure and what does it represent? At age 91 an annuitant could feel way out on a
Income Tax Act
limb if he had opted for either plan three or plan four, because both terminate at 90. The choice of that age baffles me.
I would far rather see the 90, if it has to appear at all, as a "for example." Let the annuitant decide the length of time he wants to enjoy his RRSP, but he should have explained to him all the options open to him. This is basically the role the insurance companies play-life only, fixed term only, term certain plus life, and the terms can be ten, 15, 20 or even 30 years, of course, with corresponding changes in the size of the annuity payments. As variations on these, there are joint life and term certain plus joint life when man and wife are deciding on working out their annuity as a joint operation.
I say again, in conclusion, that the RRSP owner ought to be able to get his RRSP without penalty, at least after leaving it invested for five or ten years, whenever he wants. He should be allowed to defer if he so chooses, even beyond 71, He should not be limited by the mystic age 90 either, only to find at 91 he is completely dependent on others for his everyday care.
Besides the individual criticisms, I find the broadening choice offered by the RRSP in this bill commendable. For that reason, I suppose we must commend the Minister of Finance for having such a brilliant group of public servants to bring forth these items for him, because I am sure it would not be on his own volition.

Mr. Speaker, during the past ten days we have had two special debates in the House when two opposition parties, first the Creditistes and second the Progressive Conservatives, choose a subject having to do with the economy to be debated for the day. It illustrates the importance which the opposition parties place on the fact that the economy of Canada is indeed in difficulty. The present government is doing very little to correct it and shows little concern about doing much in the future.
We have before us tonight, and have had for a number of days and, I suppose, a number of weeks, Bill C-56 which in a sense deals with the economy. This bill deals with amendments to income tax law, and sales tax in particular.
For the past several days we have heard a lot in this debate about the ridiculous proposal encompassed in this amendment involving the sales tax. I do not want to spend more time tonight on that aspect of this bill. Rather, I would like to summarize what in my view has been the general feeling around the country as to the effectiveness of Bill C-56. In particular, I want to discuss it in relation to the aspect dealing with the amendment of the sales tax.
People across this country realize that the government has shown itself to be very incompetent in the way it presented this particular cut in tax via the sales tax. Further, people realize that the government has once again shown a special status for one or more parts of this country which most of us feel is unwise. Third, there is no question but that the way they have implemented the tax with the province of Quebec is an attack on the poor which, again, the people of Canada do not appreciate seeing. Fourth, but not a bit surprising, this bill has

shown itself to be an encroachment upon the provincial rights of one or more provinces in this country. Again, we abhor that.
In summary, most Canadians disapprove of those four aspects of this bill intensely. When the next election comes, the government will realize that is the feeling of the people of Canada with regard to this bill.
I do not want to devote more time to that aspect. I would rather talk about an income tax component of this bill which I think is largely missing. What I want to say about it has to do with what might be called new thoughts or ideas on income tax and corporation tax. They are not new, but certainly are new as far as implementation of them in Canada is concerned.
I would like to put in a little brief tonight mainly on my behalf and not necessarily that of my party, because we have not discussed it at length as party policy.
It is incumbent upon all of us as legislators to play a more active role in looking at the income tax system in Canada, both at the personal and corporate level. We must try and find in that area of the economy a solution to a problem which is probably very basic to the troubles we now have with inflation, low productivity, low trade and so on. It will be found that a lot of those problems stem from our ineffective tax system.
As one looks at the total problem of taxation, one has to go back in perspective a bit. When taxes first became popular, and that is not too far back, they were levied to pay for essential services. Those taxes were levied against both corporations and individuals. As far as the individuals were concerned, the taxes were levied primarily to support functions of government such as immigration, national defence, foreign policy and other such areas where it was necessary to have a corporate body such as government look after them on behalf of the citizens.
We have gone a long way from there. We now have a government, particularly the one across the way in this House, which is no longer content with assuming that kind of control of power. They want to increase that power. They have extended their power into all sorts of other areas of involvement, into the personal life of yourself, Mr. Speaker, and that of every Canadian.
The government has shown its intense desire to take over the control and responsiblity that should reside in 90 to 95 per cent of Canadians who are quite capable of looking after themselves and do not have to be told by government how their money will be spent. We should be able to decide for ourselves rather than have a government do it.
This increasing encroachment is not only at the federal level. Many provincial and municipal governments are encroaching further and further into the power that they have to raise taxes and spend money. I want to express my personal disapproval of this and suggest, as I go along, how it can be corrected. The real role of government in this day and age should be to provide a climate for businesses which operate in this country, not to provide a very detailed, controlling influence over the Canadian people.

What is the current status of taxation in Canada? I have alluded to the fact that it is a real mess. We have all kinds of problems. I do not have to give a lot of quotations to convince hon. members of that. However, there are two or three I would like to refer to which will be supporting evidence of the difficulty we are in now as a country vis-a-vis our tax system.
Something that came out recently-and this will not be new to the parliamentary secretary whom I am pleased to see here this evening-is the report of the Royal Commission on Corporate Concentration. In its 400 pages, they do not deal mainly with taxation. However, on pages 274 and 275 the report of the Royal Commission on Corporate Concentration discusses taxation. I want to read just a few sentences to illustrate how this royal commission felt about our present tax situation.
It is abundantly clear from what we have said in this chapter that savings over the next few years will be inadequate to finance the necessary business investment and that current and expected risk-return ratios will be inadequate to induce risk capital investment. This and the other serious problems of the Canadian economy which we reviewed briefly in Chapter I concern us deeply.
The royal commission is concerned about investment in the future and that there might not be risk capital available, and I think we can supply a solution to that problem through a different tax system. The report continues as follows:
We think there must be more questioning of things that have heretofore been accepted as unchangeable. If the problems we face are as deep-seated as we think, then their solutions probably require equally fundamental changes in some of our economic arrangements. Mere tinkering with effects will not come to grips with basic underlying causes. All of us must be prepared to think about the unthinkable.
I suggest that this has been our problem with respect to taxation. We do not have any committee on either side of the House which is really concerned about taxation. We do not have any committee whose title has the word "tax" in it. I do not think any party in the House has that, which shows what little importance we attach to taxation. Nevertheless, it affects all of us in this country. The report of this royal commission says that we are going to have to have very fundamental and radical changes if we are going to get anywhere with our economy, and those changes have to be in our taxation system.
I want to read two or three more sentences which are very important because they deal directly with taxation.
It is appropriate to discuss the tax system in this chapter because a healthy, small business sector is one of the most realistic antidotes to the economic concentration that is inevitable in the Canadian economy, and which is a constant threat to competition.
I wish the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) was here tonight so that he could see some of the real challenges which exist for small business and how he might do something about them. The report continues:
The health of small business depends, more than anything else, on a vigorous economy. In addition, the measurement of taxable income and the system to collect tax on it are particularly severe problems for smaller businesses. A tax on profits is disproportionately burdensome-
I want to emphasize this because this will be the crux of my argument.

-on a small business because retained earnings are often its principal source of capital. Finally, the complexity of the tax system creates a compliance cost that the small business is least able to afford.
I do not suggest that I agree with everything in that report, but there are comments on taxation as it exists today which are indeed very apropos.
Let me quote from a speech made only two or three days ago by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke). His remarks are recorded at page 5807 of Hansard.
-I am a chartered accountant who understands, probably better than most in the House who are not chartered accountants, some of the complications in the income tax and accounting laws and I have an idea of the huge costs involved in the legal advice needed in dealing with the income tax laws.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra was suggesting that we have indeed a very complicated tax system which is causing everybody difficulty. He was implying, 1 am sure, that there need to be some changes in that.
Finally, in support of my argument that we have a very unwieldy tax system I want to quote two very short quotations from a Mr. Peter Drucker. I understand that Mr. Drucker is a world renowned expert in management consulting, and he writes on business matters. In the appendix of a book written about Mr. Drucker there are two quotations from his work. The first is: "The corporate income tax is the most asinine of taxes". The other quotation is the following: "We are dedicated to the preservation and strengthening of small business, and our tax policy is designated to destroy small business." I hope the Minister of State (Small Business) will read these little quotations because they are very apropos. This quotation continues: "Small businesses are selling out because of tax laws designed for IT & T"; that is, International Telephone and Telegraph. Here again is another quotation illustrating how ridiculous our present tax system is and the very urgent need there is to do something about it.
What is the history of taxation in Canada, and how did we get into the mess we are in now? A year or two ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that the free market system was not working. He seemed to think, for one reason or another, that the economic mess we were in then was due to the fact that the free market system did not work. He did not attempt to analyze whether it was because there was too little government involvement in the free market system or perhaps too much, but I suggest that if he had chosen to be honest with us and with everybody else, he would have told us in addition that the reason it did not work was because there had been too much government interference.
I think something has to be done along that line. The Prime Minister did his usual trick. Within a few months of his making that statement he saw fit to take the most reactionary Conservative on this side of the House over to his side of the House in order to give the impression that he was having a second thought and that perhaps the private sector needed to be encouraged a little. He brought the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) to his side to give the impression that an arch small "c", reactionary conservative could be part of the Liberal Party of Canada.

If we are to look at what has happened in our tax system, we should start back at the end of the second world war. At about that time there was a great need for fresh capital to start our industry moving again. There seemed to be a need for industry to get working more and to become more effective, and there was an apparent need for capital. A former minister who is now deceased, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, saw that in the United Kingdom there was a system known as accelerated depreciation which seemed to have an effective result as far as getting industry going again after the war. He brought this back to Canada and integrated it into our tax system. Accelerated depreciation is a form of tax relief which is nothing more than a manipulation of the tax system. As a result of that manipulation we soon developed a system in which savings were being accumulated by industry and by business because of so-called "tax incentives", and I put those words in quotation marks because there is no such thing as a tax incentive. A tax, by its very definition, is a disincentive. In any event, it was called a tax incentive, and I suppose we will have to accept that.
However, it soon became evident that companies were able to accumulate a lot of money in the way of savings, so much so that the time soon came that in its search for money to spend the government was able to auction off treasury bills and get its supply of money from what the private sector was accumulating by way of these accelerated depreciations and other tax incentives.
It was at this stage that we had the beginning of the decline in the role of profits in our basic economic system, which had functioned relatively well up until then. There was a decline in the role of the functioning of profits due to the fact that no longer did business have to borrow on the money markets, because money was then available through various types of tax incentives, accelerated depreciations, write-offs, and so forth.
One could arbitrarily say that there are two economic systems. One is based on a profit incentive. Under that type of system success in business in determined by reducing costs and by increasing productivity. I submit that it would be very difficult to find a system better than that.
Unfortunately, we have moved out of that system because of what C. D. Howe did back in the late forties or early fifties. We moved away from the profit motive being the incentive to produce and manufacture products. We got into the so-called tax incentive, which is the other type of economic system. However, under the tax incentive system the incentives do not encourage production or efficiency. Incentives are there to inflate costs. The greater the costs, the more successful a business can be.
We have the anomalous situation in our economy where presumably we are trying to produce more, put more people to

As a result of that, business becomes subservient to government, and I suggest that the present government-and, I suspect, other governments in this country-enjoys the feeling of power it has over the corporate sector.
